analysis.one_liner: Bars the FCC from issuing any new regulations on the internet or internet-based services.
analysis.headline: Senator McCain's bill to strip the FCC of its authority over the internet was referred to committee in October 2009, never received a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the Federal Communications Commission from writing any rules about the internet or internet-based services, with narrow exceptions for national security, public safety, law enforcement, and the universal phone-subsidy fund. It was introduced as the FCC was preparing its first net neutrality rules, which would stop internet providers from blocking or slowing websites or charging companies for faster delivery. The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee and never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband and wireless internet providers. Without FCC rules, they could block, slow down, or prioritize internet traffic as they saw fit — including charging websites and streaming services extra fees for faster delivery to customers, and deciding which services users can reach.

how_it_helps.text: The bill flatly prohibits the FCC from proposing, issuing, or adopting any regulations regarding the internet or IP-enabled services.
It carves out only four exceptions: national security, public safety, assisting law enforcement, and keeping the Universal Service Fund solvent.
It declares that internet and IP-enabled services are not subject to the jurisdiction of any state or local government, blocking state-level internet rules as well.

analysis.who_pays: Internet users and the websites and services they rely on. Without an open-internet rule, home internet providers could charge online companies for priority delivery — costs likely passed to consumers — and could favor their own services or paying partners over others. Small websites and startups, which cannot pay for priority, would compete on unequal terms.

drawbacks.text: Broadband providers argued that FCC regulation would deter investment in network buildout, since companies are less likely to spend billions upgrading networks if the government can set the terms of how those networks are used. An honest supporter of net neutrality rules acknowledges that heavy-handed rules can slow deployment if written poorly.
The bill was written as a total ban rather than a balanced framework: it gives the FCC no ability to address even noncontroversial consumer harms online unless they fit one of four narrow exceptions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit flows almost entirely to large internet providers, who gain freedom from open-internet rules and keep the power to charge for priority access. The cost falls on everyday internet users, who would lose the guarantee that their provider delivers all websites equally. Given that the bill banned regulation wholesale rather than crafting a narrower investment-protection compromise, its costs to the public outweighed its benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in October 2009, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the Internet Freedom Act of 2009 on October 22, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

The bill would have prohibited the FCC from proposing, promulgating, or issuing any regulations regarding the internet or IP-enabled services, except for rules tied to national security, public safety, law enforcement, or the solvency of the Universal Service Fund.

No further action was ever taken: the complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral, with no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.
The bill's six cosponsors were all Senate Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyday internet users came out ahead. Because the bill died, the FCC kept its authority and went on to adopt its first open-internet (net neutrality) rules, while broadband providers failed to strip that authority by statute.

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Jay Rockefeller
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; the complete action history shows nothing after the October 2009 referral.

against.name: Federal Communications Commission (FCC)
against.what_they_did: Was moving forward with an open-internet (net neutrality) rulemaking at the time, the very activity the bill sought to prohibit.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter was a Senate Republican — the sponsor plus 6 of the chamber's 40 Republicans — with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill died in the Democratic-led Commerce Committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Broadband and wireless internet providers (cable and phone companies)
industries.note: The bill would have permanently barred the FCC from adopting open-internet rules, leaving providers free to block, slow, or prioritize traffic and to charge websites for faster delivery. Their gain came directly at the expense of the openness of the internet for ordinary users.

industries.industry: Websites, streaming services, and online businesses (edge providers)
industries.note: These companies rely on equal access to customers over broadband networks. Without FCC rules, they could have been charged for priority or deprioritized against competitors, with costs passed to users.
